| [THEORY-1108](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1108.md) | On Imachi and colleagues' cultivation of Candidatus Prometheoarchaeum syntrophicum MK-D1, the first Asgard archaeon grown in the laboratory is a small, internally simple coccus with long branching protrusions that degrades amino acids only in syntrophy, handing hydrogen and formate to partners that can be exchanged, and from its genome and other Asgard genomes the authors infer that the Asgard ancestor was likewise dependent on metabolic partners; the isolate is a modern relative separated from the host lineage by about two billion years, grown only in co-culture, and the entangle–engulf–endogenize model built on it is a hypothesis the authors call not definitive | Imachi et al. (2020), [LIT-1591](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1591.md), read in [NOTE-1238](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1238.md). Partner inhibitors impair MK-D1's growth, added hydrogen or formate stops it, and it grows with either of two methanogens, so its dependence is on a service that several partners can supply. Cryo-EM and TEM show no internal compartments. The step from this one organism to the Asgard ancestor is a genomic inference, which the authors hedge. The sharp edge for the record is that the most famous transition in individuality may have begun from a host already dependent on others, with no partner specificity, cohesion or control. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1109](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1109.md) | Santana-Molina, Williams, Snel and Spang find that the last eukaryotic common ancestor's central carbon metabolism was chimeric: a few Asgard-archaeal enzymes in cytosolic glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, most alphaproteobacterial ones in the mitochondrial TCA cycle and pyruvate conversion, and others from various bacteria with no third dominant donor, since remodelled by loss, horizontal replacement and retargeting so that compartment no longer follows origin; the authors take the cytosol–mitochondrion split as support for syntrophy, but it is what any archaeal-host, bacterial-endosymbiont origin would leave | Santana-Molina, Williams, Snel & Spang (2025), [LIT-1564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1564.md), read in [NOTE-1239](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1239.md). LECA had a complete central carbon metabolism. Six enzymes are placed with Asgard archaea, mostly cytosolic (bootstrap 39–97%, two ambiguous). Seventeen are alphaproteobacterial, ten of them in the TCA cycle, mostly mitochondrial. Others come from several bacteria, none dominant. Since LECA, Asgard enzymes have been replaced in many lineages and enzymes retargeted regardless of origin. The authors read the split as support for syntrophy; it does not discriminate syntrophy from other symbiogenetic models. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1111](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1111.md) | Spectators' identification with football clubs varies on two independent axes, how central the club is to the self (hot or cool) and whether the tie rests on local tradition or on market consumption, giving supporters, followers, fans and flâneurs; and commodification since the late 1980s has shifted identification from supporters towards flâneurs | Giulianotti (2002), [LIT-1150](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1150.md), read from the author's pre-review text. Four ideal types: supporters (traditional/hot: kin-like, topophilic, obligatory), followers (traditional/cool: nested, mediated allegiances), fans (consumer/hot: non-reciprocal intimacy, authenticated by consumption) and flâneurs (consumer/cool: cosmopolitan window-shoppers of clubs). Hypercommodification is said to move identification from supporter towards flâneur, while the spectacle flâneurs consume depends on supporters. Proposed: a conceptual classification with no data, and a trend claim that is asserted, not measured. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1112](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1112.md) | Perceiving people as a group entity, rather than as members of a common category, requires detecting or inferring collective intentionality among them; similarity, and categorization into an equivalence class, yields interchangeable members but not a group | Skorich (2025, v2 2026), [LIT-1765](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1765.md), a preprint. Categorization with accentuation makes members interchangeable, not one, since a category is a set and a set is internally differentiated. Groups such as orchestras and families need no similarity. Groups are holistic entities perceived from cues to shared mental states, much as faces are perceived from configuration. Reported support: four experiments under review in which groups defined by a mental state (a chosen T-shirt colour; seeing the duck or the rabbit) drew more favouritism and tracking than groups defined by a physical property. Proposed: the argument is conceptual and the evidence is unpublished. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1113](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1113.md) | In team-sport fandom, perceived rivalry intensity lowers fans' sense of being respected by the rival's fans but raises their sense of in-group distinctiveness and cohesion, and these gains run through the perception that the rivalry is reciprocated, not through disidentification with the rival | Berendt & Uhrich (2016), [LIT-1147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1147.md): an SEM of 571 Bundesliga stadium attendees. Rivalry intensity: public collective self-esteem relative to the rival's fans −.31. Perceived distinctiveness +.27, cohesion +.20, and regard from other clubs' fans +.09, with direct paths null and indirect effects via perceived reciprocity .18–.20. Disidentification carries almost none. Proposed: one cross-sectional sample, a single-item predictor, a new reciprocity scale, and causal order assumed by the model. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1114](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1114.md) v2 | Which self-category a person uses, what it means and who in it is most typical vary lawfully with the comparative frame of reference: a grouping of self with others becomes salient as the differences within it shrink relative to the differences between it and the rest of the frame (metacontrast) and as those differences match expectations about the category, and as it does, self-perception is depersonalized | Self-categorization theory as restated by Turner, Oakes, Haslam and McGarty (1994), [LIT-1794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1794.md), and reviewed by Hornsey (2008), [LIT-1742](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1742.md). Personal and social identity are levels of self-categorization. Salience is perceiver readiness times fit, comparative fit being the metacontrast ratio. The level, kind, content and prototype structure of self-categories shift with the comparison set: Americans read as less aggressive beside Iraq than beside the Soviet Union, and a group's extreme members become more prototypical in an intergroup context. Proposed: every result in the record comes through the theory's authors, reported without data, and the account's stronger claim, that the self is generated rather than stored, is not part of it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1115](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1115.md) | A we-identity, being one of us, can arise through mutual individualization, in which members grasp one another as non-substitutable and complementary, without depersonalization, as in long friendships and romantic partnerships; so depersonalization is not necessary for a we-identity | León (2023), [LIT-1721](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1721.md). Self-categorization theory claims depersonalization as "the basic process underlying group phenomena", for groups of any size, friendship groups included (Turner et al. 1987, pp. 50, 103, as quoted), and phenomenologists have taken it as the account of the "we". But close relationships yield we-identities while their members grasp each other as non-substitutable, and relationship research on couple resilience finds the "we" more adaptive the more differentiated the "I". Proposed: the argument is conceptual, and the cited evidence was not analysed by the source or read here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1116](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1116.md) | Football fans can identify with a superordinate community of fans across clubs and countries, a European fan community, alongside their club identity rather than in place of it; that identification goes with particularized trust in foreign fans and cross-border viewing, and is independent of attitudes to the sport's governing institutions | Biel (2026), [LIT-1133](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1133.md): a four-country quota survey of 3,685 fans. Club, national and European fan-community identification average 6.1, 5.6 and 5.3 of 10. The European item loads on its own factor in a two-factor solution. It goes with trust in a European fan from elsewhere (b = .34), viewing of foreign leagues, positive views of fans and attachment to Europe, and not with critique of football governance. Proposed: single items, a Heywood case in the factor solution, percentages whose denominator does not match the analysed n, and cross-sectional associations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1120.md) | For LLM translations of culturally loaded Indic utterances into English, the reference-based COMET metric agrees with a native speaker's pragmatic-adequacy rating at r ≈ 0.81 overall, better than XCOMET or MetricX, yet scores some pragmatically inverted outputs highly | Singh et al. (2026), [LIT-1817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1817.md), read in [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md). On 416 outputs (104 items × 4 models), wmt22 COMET correlates with 1–5 pragmatic-adequacy scores at Pearson 0.813, Spearman 0.860; XCOMET ρ 0.792, MetricX ρ 0.788 (Table 3). Four hand-picked outputs scored 0.65–0.86 by COMET and 1–2 by the rater. Each language had one rater, so there is no reliability against which to read 0.81, and the claim that metrics fail "especially for implicature and deixis" rests on per-phenomenon differences of 0.1 or less. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1124](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1124.md) | Normalized log co-occurrences of words in large corpora behave as distances in a Euclidean semantic space: they correlate with human similarity ratings (r = 0.75 against MEN) and their nearest-neighbour centrality and reciprocity fall in the range expected of points sampled in a Euclidean space, apart from superordinate and function words | Hashimoto, Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2016), [LIT-1801](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1801.md), §3, read in [NOTE-1329](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1329.md). The correlation follows a normalization chosen to maximize it; the two nearest-neighbour statistics are necessary conditions, the corpora exceed the asymptotic centrality bound and pass only a non-asymptotic range, and the free-association data fail the reciprocity criterion the paper states. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1126](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1126.md) | In animal development the organ-level outcome is reproducible while the trajectories of individual cells differ between embryos raised alike, so developmental regularity is imposed on variable cell behaviour rather than read out from a fixed sequence of cellular events (Weiss, as Nicholson reconstructs him), with invariant lineages such as that of C. elegans the conceded exception | Nicholson (2026), [LIT-1821](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1821.md), read in [NOTE-1340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1340.md). Weiss's "determinacy in the gross despite demonstrable indeterminacy in the small", shown as a redrawn schematic (Fig. 5) and supported by citations to work on stochastic gene expression and cell-fate decisions. This is the only one of the paper's four critiques that rests on evidence, and the paper presents none of the evidence itself. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1127.md) | A CycleGAN trained to translate aerial photographs to maps and back satisfies its cycle-consistency loss by encoding details of the photograph in a low-amplitude, high-frequency signal in the generated map: the reconstruction recovers details the visible map lacks, is destroyed by noise of three 8-bit levels or by JPEG compression and survives low-frequency change, and the same sensitivity lets an imperceptible perturbation of almost any map make the reverse generator output any chosen photograph | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler (2017), [LIT-1800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1800.md), §§2–4, read in [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md). One trained model on one dataset. The noise curve (Fig. 3, 50 photographs) is the only quantitative result; the hidden details, the composing edits and the attack are shown by examples. Proposed: an empirical finding about one model, said by the authors to recur on other datasets, not shown. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1131](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1131.md) | On native-authored pragmatic items in Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Malayalam, current multilingual LLMs pick the right reading from four options more often than they label it unaided, and when wrong they lean toward the literal reading | Singh et al. (2026), [LIT-1817](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1817.md), read in [NOTE-1345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1345.md) from the Findings of EMNLP 2026 PDF. MCQ beat NLI in 20 of 20 model–language pairs (recomputed). 59.1% of wrong MCQ answers took the literal distractor, against 33.3% by chance, and 53.8% of Contradiction items were labelled Entailment. The gold answers are each language's one item author's reading, cells hold 5–16 items, and the MCQ and NLI sets are different items. So "recognizing and reasoning about pragmatic meaning are distinct competencies" is the authors' gloss, not a finding. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1134.md) | A translation metric that predicts a sentence score and token-level error spans from one shared encoder reaches segment-level agreement with expert MQM annotation of Kendall τ about 0.4 and span F1 under 0.33, the best among open metrics and GPT-4 prompting at the time, while its score and its own spans agree with each other at Pearson 0.73 to 0.92, so the explanation it gives is far more coherent with its score than either is with the human judgement | Guerreiro, Rei, van Stigt, Coheur, Colombo and Martins (TACL 2024), [LIT-1816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1816.md), Tables 2, 4 and 5, read in [NOTE-1341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1341.md). The numbers are the paper's, on WMT22 News MQM (zh-en, en-de, en-ru). The paper reads the heads' agreement as support for the spans as explanation; the record reads it as coherence. The top of the agreement, 0.90–0.92, is partly arithmetic, since the final score includes the span score with weight 2/9. Proposed: one test set, and the comparison is across different statistics (Pearson between heads, Kendall and F1 against humans). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1136](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1136.md) | Poincaré embeddings of one hierarchy from different random seeds differ by more than an isometry of the hyperbolic ball, with branches placed differently and pairwise distances changed, so aligners that allow only a global orthogonal or Möbius map recover almost none of the correspondence, while a non-linear registration by a hyperbolic neural network, trained through a Sinkhorn divergence and started from a pretraining step, recovers a substantial part of it but finds the exact match for under a quarter of items even when the two hierarchies are identical | Alvarez-Melis, Mroueh and Jaakkola (2020), [LIT-1808](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1808.md), §§5–7, Figs. 1–2, Tables 1–2; read in [NOTE-1323](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1323.md). Proposed: single runs, one embedding method for the matching experiments, and GW, the obvious isometry-free baseline, is not run. It does not say why seeds disagree (the paper conjectures negative sampling), nor that the matching preserves the hierarchy's direction, which it does not enforce. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1137](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1137.md) | When an abstraction map between two causal models is learned by optimal transport from paired interventional distributions, a transport cost that rewards pairs of states compatible with the same paired interventions gives much lower held-out abstraction error than a Hamming cost when the intervention set is rich, and higher error when it holds only a few, because with few interventions the compatibility cost is nearly uniform | Felekis et al. (CLeaR 2024), [LIT-1806](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1806.md), §§4.2 and 6 and Appendices C and E, read in [NOTE-1342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1342.md). Two synthetic models (STC, LUCAS) and one real two-lab dataset (EBM), all discrete, evaluated by leaving one intervention pair out. The ω-cost wins on STC with parent-free interventions and on LUCAS, loses on STC with two interventions on tar and on EBM. The explanation, a nearly uniform cost when interventions are few, is argued and fits the four cases. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1139](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1139.md) | A graph network that learns its sheaf restriction maps from node features at each layer reaches the top of the standard small heterophilic node-classification benchmarks and stays within about one point of the best on homophilic ones; on a synthetic balanced bipartite graph it learns the negative transport the theory prescribes, but whether the maps it learns on real graphs have the geometry the theory credits for its success has not been examined | Bodnar et al. (NeurIPS 2022), [LIT-1811](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1811.md), §§5–6 and Appendix F, read in [NOTE-1332](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1332.md). The results are empirical: Table 1 on nine datasets of 183 to 18,717 nodes with ten fixed splits, baselines copied from earlier papers, spreads of one to nine points; and one synthetic bipartite experiment in which the learned maps are inspected. Proposed: the paper's explanation of its accuracy, that the model learns the right geometry, is tested only on the synthetic case. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1143](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1143.md) | When one domain carries more information than the other, a translation trained only to make the round trip close cannot meet that requirement through a correspondence in the intermediate's visible code, so the round trip closes through a channel the intermediate's audience does not read; agreement of the round trip with its source therefore says nothing about whether the intermediate renders the source's content for that audience | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler (2017), [LIT-1800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1800.md), §2 and §5, read in [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md). The authors argue it from the many photographs a single map stands for, and support it with [THEORY-1127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1127.md)'s evidence on one model; they propose, and do not run, the test of adding capacity to the smaller domain. Proposed. It is the converse of the record's collapse case for [CLAIM-496](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-496.md): there routes agree because nothing travels, here because everything does, out of sight. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1144](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1144.md) | A multilingual classifier trained only on English politeness ratings separates the most from the least polite requests in nine other languages at about 81% accuracy, without translation, yet stays about 10 points below one native judge's agreement with two others in most of them | Srinivasan and Choi (2022), [LIT-1799](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1799.md), read in [NOTE-1339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1339.md). XLM-R fine-tuned on 1,926 English requests reaches 0.808 mean accuracy on the balanced top/bottom-quartile sets (250 per language), 0.801 on Google Translate input; GPT-3 zero-shot 0.706 (Table 3). Leave-one-out human accuracy is around 90% (Fig. 3). The judges were screened for agreeing with this classifier, and the extreme items were chosen on a mean that includes the held-out judge, so the gap and the transfer are both measured on favourable ground. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1145](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1145.md) | Unsupervised alignment of two monolingual word-embedding spaces recovers translations only where the spaces are close to isometric, and the distance from isometry depends on the corpora and the embedding algorithm as well as on the languages: adversarial alignment fails for English with Estonian or Finnish, across corpus domains, and between skip-gram and CBOW spaces of the same language pair, GW alignment is weakest on the same Finnish pair, and a spectral dissimilarity of small nearest-neighbour graphs tracks success | Søgaard, Ruder and Vulić (2018), [LIT-1819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1819.md), read in [NOTE-1337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1337.md), with the GW results of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), [LIT-1818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1818.md), read in [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md). Proposed: the evidence is single runs of one adversarial method, plus one GW table, and the authors themselves report that some seeds succeed where the method otherwise fails. What it does not support is a typological law about dependent marking, or the reading that a good fit establishes that the matched words mean the same. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1146](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1146.md) | Under confounding the partition of a variable X by what it predicts about a target Y differs from its partition by what setting it does to Y, so the information bottleneck at full sufficiency learns distinctions no intervention could use and misses ones only intervention reveals, while the causal information bottleneck, computed from observational data through a backdoor set, recovers the causal partition; in three toy models projected gradient search found it in 95 to 100 percent of runs | Simoes, Dastani and van Ommen (UAI 2025), [LIT-1802](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1802.md), §8 and Appendices E–F, read in [NOTE-1347](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1347.md). Three SCMs with 7, 4 and 16 values of X; ensembles of 4 to 12 optimisers; a penalty against unused values of T was needed at full control. The difference between the partitions follows from the definitions; what the experiments add is that the search finds the causal one. Proposed: toy problems only. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1148](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1148.md) | Single judges agree moderately on how pragmatically similar two spoken utterances are, mean pairwise correlation 0.45 to 0.72 by session, less when the utterances differ in words, so a mean over six to nine judges is much more reliable than any one judge | Ward and Marco (2024), [LIT-1812](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1812.md), read in [NOTE-1338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1338.md) from the LREC-COLING 2024 PDF. Over 693 seed/re-enactment pairs in three sessions, mean pairwise Pearson agreement was 0.45, 0.72 and 0.66 (Table 2), and 0.80 in Session 2 when lexically different pairs were left out (p. 160). The Spearman–Brown reliability of the panel means, 0.88–0.96, is my computation. The judges talked during the session and knew each other, and all pairs are within one language, so the figure is neither a floor for a panel nor a value for translations. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1151](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1151.md) | A learned translation metric trained with synthetic hallucinations and diagnostic perturbations alongside human MQM flags most injected localized critical errors (all but 0 to 17 percent, by type and model size) and ranks fully detached hallucinations below other translations with AUROC up to 0.96, and without a reference it ranks hallucinations better than with one; how far this reflects the synthetic training data has not been separated from how far it generalises | Guerreiro et al. (TACL 2024), [LIT-1816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1816.md), §7 (Tables 6 and 8, Fig. 4), read in [NOTE-1341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1341.md). Localized errors are SMAUG perturbations of English references; hallucinations are one de-en benchmark of real system outputs. The training data includes synthetic detached and oscillatory hallucinations and DEMETR perturbations. The localized-error table's "All" row is inconsistent with its rows. The larger model is worse on oscillatory hallucinations. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1153](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1153.md) | In English-source TED and Europarl translations, the additions a translator makes for the target audience that a named-entity and null-alignment filter can find are mostly unit conversions and entity descriptions or specifications, and their mix differs by target language | Osmelak et al. (2026), [LIT-1798](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1798.md), read in [NOTE-1344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1344.md) from the LREC 2026 PDF. Of 3,754 type instances in Table 2, 1,722 are system transfers (mostly measurement conversion) and 992 entity changes; the mix varies by language. It is a count over a pool selected by a filter that requires a named entity, mostly found by a classifier, labelled with no reported agreement. It is not a base rate of explicitation in translation, and it says nothing about how readers take the additions. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1154](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1154.md) | People interpreting an analogy carry relations from base to target and drop the attributes of objects, and among the relations they prefer those bound into a system by higher-order relations, such as causal or mathematical constraints, over isolated ones (structure-mapping and its systematicity principle) | Gentner (1983), [LIT-1810](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1810.md), read in [NOTE-1349](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1349.md). Argued from worked examples (the Rutherford analogy, heat and water) with one study, summarized without statistics, showing relational content dominating interpretations of analogies but not descriptions of objects. The systematicity principle is stated as a likelihood on p. 163 and as determination in the abstract and summary. The rules work on a predicate structure the theory takes as given, which its footnote 4 concedes is a modelling choice. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1157](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1157.md) | Native-speaker crowd judges agree only modestly on the graded politeness of written requests in their own language, mean pairwise Spearman about 0.46 across nine languages, and the same bilinguals agree less on English requests, about 0.36 | Srinivasan and Choi (2022), [LIT-1799](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1799.md), read in [NOTE-1339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1339.md) from the Findings of EMNLP 2022 PDF. Three Prolific annotators per item rated Wikipedia requests −3 to +3; mean pairwise Spearman within 20-item tasks was 0.46 on the 15 target-language items and 0.36 on the 5 English items (Table 2). The paper says own-language agreement is higher "across all nine languages"; Tamil (0.33 against 0.38) is the exception. The annotators had been screened for agreeing with an XLM-R classifier. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1158](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1158.md) | On synchronization of S4 relations with outliers, an untrained mechanism that composes relations through third vertices gains 26–45 points over the single direct path, and weighting the candidate paths by the Wilson loops of squares that avoid the missing edge adds 0.6–7.8 points, most where clean two-hop paths become a minority, without beating spectral synchronization; its 0.99 AUC for corrupted triangles is the ceiling that exactly flat clean data set, not a measure of detection power | Sarkar, Mukherjee and Sato (2026), [LIT-1820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1820.md), §3 and Table 1, read in [NOTE-1331](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1331.md). The accuracies are the paper's, on 1000 instances per cell, and were not rerun. The AUC ceiling was recomputed here: 1.42% of corrupted triangles at p = 0.3 have cancelling corruptions, so the ceiling is 0.9929. What the experiment does not show is anything about learned operators, language, or relations not given as group elements. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1159](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1159.md) | Aligning three networks jointly, through one multi-marginal fused Gromov–Wasserstein coupling with an anchor-based random-walk cost and a cluster decomposition, finds held-out correspondences better than pairwise and existing multi-network methods, in both pairwise and whole-tuple hits, on benchmarks whose true correspondences are consistent across the three networks by construction; whether the joint coupling itself is the cause is not separated from the new cost and the clustering | Zeng et al. (2024), [LIT-1814](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1814.md), §5 and Appendix C, read in [NOTE-1334](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1334.md). Reported as plots against 13 baselines on ER, Douban, DBLP and ACM triples, with 10% anchors and 90% held out. Proposed: the result is empirical, its ground truth is a consistent set of node triples, and no ablation holds the cost and the clustering fixed while changing joint for pairwise fitting. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1160](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1160.md) | Choosing which source objects to have an oracle match, by the derivative of a proxy utility of the entropic transport plan (its nearness to a permutation, or its consistency with the graphs) with respect to supervising each candidate match, averaged over matches by the current plan, raises held-out alignment accuracy more than uncertainty, centrality and matching-sampling query rules at the same label budget, by up to about three points on network alignment and less on image–text tasks; the gain depends on weighting by the current plan, without which the rule does worse than random | Yu et al. (2026), [LIT-1807](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1807.md), Tables 3–5 and 7, read in [NOTE-1327](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1327.md). Eight datasets, four aligners, a budget of 20% of true pairs in ten rounds after a random 20%, five runs, no variances. Proposed: an empirical result with small margins, on benchmarks where the truth is near one-to-one, so a coherence proxy and accuracy agree. It chooses among fixed questions; it does not extend what can be asked. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1161](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1161.md) | Under reflected appraisal across issues, whether power concentrates in one member depends on the single-issue step: with Friedkin–Johnsen anchoring on initial positions almost every random strongly connected group evolves to a single leader, and with DeGroot consensus the same random complete networks keep power spread | Friedkin (2011/2012), [LIT-1404](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1404.md), and Jia et al. (2015), [LIT-1146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1146.md), use the same reflected-appraisal rule, the next self-weight set to the member's share of control over the last issue, and different single-issue steps. Friedkin's anchored step gives a single leader in over 98% of 100,000 random networks; the DeGroot step gives one non-autocratic equilibrium except on a star. A re-run on the same networks bears out the contrast. It does not say which step real groups follow, and Friedkin's experiment cannot tell. | Proposed |
